articleTitle: Number-plate matching for automatic vehicle identification
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: The continuing increase in the number of vehicle related offences has generated a wave of interest by law enforcement agencies, in investigating the use of automatic vehicle identification (AVI) techniques for apprehending/prosecuting offenders. The authors have outlined how number plate matching could be effectively used, possibly in conjunction with conventional technologies, in the prevention, detection, and solution of crime. The measures taken to minimise some problems in number plate matching and hence improve on the character recognition capability have also been discussed. Initial experiments in the implementation of these algorithms indicate that very high success rates are possible with this approach.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Facial recognition for police purposes using computer graphics and neural networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: Neural nets provide a viable solution to identifying criminals photographed at the scene of the crime. A program was written in lightspeed Pascal on a Macintosh II personal computer to simulate a WISARD neural network. A target face from the photograph collection was chosen at random and the net was trained to recognise it. The experimental work is outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer vision for security surveillance and movement control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: The authors report the application of several different parallel algorithms to detect and track moving objects in indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. The algorithms are coded in the Occam language and run in a transputer image processing system (TIPS) which has been designed and built in the Faculty of Engineering at Bristol University.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: The authors concentrate on three main areas of biometric measurements which are covered by their integrated database. They are: speech recognition, signature recognition and face recognition. The specific requirements for each of these human identification methods are described in detail with reference to their applications such as personal identification checks during cheque guaranteeing, secured premises entry/access and delivered items acceptance. The data acquisition control aspects and the present state of the project are outlined. Some illustrative pictorial examples of images from the database are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer reconstruction of 2-D photographs from alternative viewpoints
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: The reconstruction of mug-shots from various angles has obvious advantages where witnesses are attempting to identify a subject who may have been observed from a viewpoint other than that recorded on a frontal photograph. Alternatively, the ability to modify a frontal photograph in such a way that it allows reconciliation of the photograph and views of the subject as seen by witnesses from different viewpoints, has the potential to lead to a more accurate description of the subject being obtained. Both of these applications are facilitated by a computer graphics technique described, in which an image, held in computer memory, of a frontal facial photograph, is texture mapped onto the surface of an underlying 3D skeletal model.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Polarimetric image processing: an important new tool for forensic science
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: The author describes a powerful visual probing technique which could be of benefit to forensic scientists. Whenever electromagnetic radiation is reflected from a surface, it becomes polarised to a degree, dependent upon surface structure, texture and angle of incidence. If the polarisation information from the reflected radiation is extracted from conventional intensity information by an imaging polarimeter it is possible to reveal detail about the surface that cannot be obtained by any other imaging technique. An imaging polarimeter produces images representing the spatial variation in polarisation over the scene, which can be related to true texture, surface structure and material type. To provide an adequate perspective on the capability of an imaging polarimeter, and how polarimetry could become an important technique for forensic science, the relevant theoretical basis for the processing of polarimetric images is presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A new approach to face composites construction: superimposition of whole face images
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: The authors describe a computerized system for the construction of face composites, which covers witness interviewing, the composite construction, and a mugsearch using the resulting composite. The system has three major stages: In the first, the witness chooses the photos most similar to the suspect from amongst a large album. In the second stage, the computer presents the witness with various average combinations of the photos, to chose the best representation of the suspect (either one of the original photos or one of the averages). In the third stage, the witness uses image editing techniques such as cutting and pasting and drawing in order to further improve the composite.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Images and Image Processing in Security and Forensic Science
abstract: The wide-spread use of single-strike carbon typewriter ribbons, from which typed text can be read directly, provides investigators with a potential source of evidence and information. However, reading and transcribing these ribbons manually is both difficult and extremely labour intensive. Industrial Monitoring Equipment Limited has developed a ribbon transcription vision system in order to overcome this problem. The RAW-1 ribbon analysis workstation is a computer driven system designed to enable specialists in questioned documents to transcribe and analyse any of the wide range of single-strike, film typewriter ribbons in a vastly reduced period of time compared with that currently taken. During this operation operator involvement and handling are both reduced to a minimum and the resultant print-out displays everything on the original ribbon, including typing errors and blemishes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
